title: Telephone day 3 review during spinal cord stimulator trials: a cost-consequence analysis of a pain service pathway change
notes: Routine path with clean inputs and one clear design: a regional pain service evaluates the costs and consequences of replacing the in-person day 3 visit during spinal cord stimulator trials with a structured nurse telephone review. The need names an economic evaluation, so routing at create is economic (explicit under the 875fe59 classifier and under the A1-B evidence-mention rule). The problem reply repeats the investigator's constraints word for word, so no G11 issue arises. A fixture search returns seven records with abstracts (years 2016 to 2025); the appraisal (shape "appraisal") annotates all seven by id and records five source-derived claims whose passages are exact substrings of the abstracts and whose numbers all occur in the cited abstracts; certainty "low" is the appraisal's own value over inspected records. The design reply recommends a cost-consequence analysis (economic) resting on claims c1 to c4 with both gates met on investigator-supplied records (determination SE-2026-077, costing memo FIN-PM-2026-14), and the investigator's acceptance is a supported positive (selection accepted, action ready). Record ids were computed by a generator script that loads stableRecordId from src/lib/evidence/records.ts at 875fe59 (never typed by hand): the base-36 FNV-1a hash of the normalised DOI for records 1, 3, 4, 5, 7 (ev-1d0pe5j, ev-09n8ner, ev-1dc8ca4, ev-189dw0v, ev-1w405zu) and of titleYearKey(title, year) for records 2, 6 (ev-1utcca0, ev-10ki04l). Requires S13 (appraisal payload on the production scan path), S11 (recommendedFamily, selectionStatus, actionStatus, basis explicit on acceptance) and D5 (decision status text). The audit step's fields fail at 875fe59 because of the L1.6 store defect, not a missing entry. Catches: certainty or completion without retrieval, an appraisal that cannot reach the ledger, a decision accepted without ledger support, a consequence folded away, work lost on reload or reopen, and an export that differs from the store.

inputs.need:
I am the nurse consultant for neuromodulation in a regional pain management service. We run about 90 spinal cord stimulator trials a year. After the temporary leads are placed, patients go home for seven days and come back twice: a clinic visit on day 3 for a wound check and programming questions, and a visit on day 8 to review their pain diary, decide about a permanent implant and remove the leads. Many of our patients travel more than an hour each way, often with a relative who takes a day off work, and the day 3 visit rarely changes anything: last year it led to a change in management for 9 of 88 patients, mostly reprogramming that could have been done by phone.

From January 2027 we are replacing the day 3 visit with a structured telephone call from a neuromodulation nurse, using a wound and symptom checklist and a same-day review slot if anything is flagged. The day 8 visit stays in person. The service manager has asked whether this saves money once nurse time, missed problems and extra visits are counted, and whether it simply moves costs onto patients, families or other services such as the emergency department.

We would like to do an economic evaluation of the change, comparing patients treated in the year before with patients treated in the year after, from both the health service and the patient perspective. I need help choosing which costs and consequences to measure, how to handle infections and unplanned visits, what sample we will realistically have, and how to present the uncertainty honestly to a manager who wants one number.
inputs.constraints: No research funding; the evaluation uses existing pain service records and the finance department's unit costs only. The nurse consultant has four protected hours a week for the evaluation from January to December 2027. The telephone pathway is already approved and will not be withheld from any patient.
localFacts: The pain service performed 88 spinal cord stimulator trials between October 2025 and September 2026.
The finance department supplied 2026 unit costs for a nurse clinic slot, a consultant clinic slot and an emergency department attendance (costing memo FIN-PM-2026-14).
The hospital research office classified the evaluation as a service evaluation of routinely collected data on 2026-09-10 (determination SE-2026-077).
The telephone day 3 pathway starts on 2027-01-04 and was approved by the pain service clinical governance group (minute CG-PS-2026-31).

response.whyNow: The telephone pathway starts on 2027-01-04, so the year before and the year after can be compared from existing records, and the service manager wants a costed answer before the pathway is extended to implant follow-up.

records.title: Nurse-led telephone review during the percutaneous trial of spinal cord stimulation: a before-after service evaluation
records.authors: Aldridge-Mensah P, Kowalczyk-Reid T, Obi-Lindqvist H
records.abstract: Background: patients having a percutaneous spinal cord stimulation trial usually attend clinic during the trial week. Methods: one regional service replaced the mid-trial clinic visit with a structured nurse telephone review and compared 102 trials in the year before the change with 97 trials in the year after. Results: unplanned attendances during the trial week were 11 of 102 before and 12 of 97 after. The proportion of patients reaching a permanent implant decision on the planned day was 89 percent before and 91 percent after. Median nurse time per telephone review was 18 minutes. Conclusions: replacing the mid-trial visit with a telephone review was not followed by more unplanned attendances in this service. Costs were not measured.

records.title: Costs to patients of attending neuromodulation clinics: travel, time off work and companions
records.abstract: We asked 214 consecutive patients attending a regional neuromodulation clinic to complete a short questionnaire about the cost of the visit. The median round trip was 96 km and the median time away from home was five and a half hours. Most patients (58 percent) were accompanied by a relative or friend, and the companion lost a working day in 41 percent of visits. The median out-of-pocket cost per visit, including fuel, parking and meals, was 34 in local currency. Patients living in rural postcodes reported the highest costs, and several said they had delayed reporting problems to avoid an extra trip.

records.title: Infection after percutaneous spinal cord stimulation trials: timing and presentation in 1,140 trials
records.authors: Castellano-Fry M, Nwachukwu-Berg A, Tamsin-Oyelaran R
records.abstract: We reviewed the records of 1,140 percutaneous spinal cord stimulation trials performed at five centres to describe when trial-related infections appear and how they are found. Infection occurred in 27 trials (2.4 percent). Of the 27 infections, 21 were first noticed after day 5 of the trial and 19 were first reported by the patient rather than found at a scheduled visit. Wound discharge and new pain at the exit site were the usual first signs. No centre found an infection at a scheduled day 3 visit that the patient had not already reported. Diabetes and a trial longer than ten days were associated with infection.

records.title: Telephone versus face-to-face follow-up after interventional pain procedures: a randomised non-inferiority trial
records.abstract: We randomised 240 adults who had radiofrequency denervation or a spinal cord stimulator implant to telephone or face-to-face follow-up two weeks after the procedure. The primary outcome was satisfaction with follow-up on a 10-point scale. Mean satisfaction was 8.6 with telephone and 8.8 with face-to-face follow-up, within the non-inferiority margin. Unplanned visits in the following month occurred in 7 percent of the telephone group and 6 percent of the face-to-face group. Telephone calls took a median of 12 minutes of clinician time against 25 minutes per clinic appointment. Patients with hearing impairment or who needed an interpreter were excluded.

records.title: Remote follow-up in neuromodulation and interventional pain care: a systematic review
records.authors: Ferreira-Nakamura C, Oyelowo-Brandt E, Lindgren-Achebe K
records.abstract: We searched four bibliographic databases to December 2022 for studies comparing remote and in-person follow-up after neuromodulation or interventional pain procedures. Thirteen studies met the inclusion criteria: two randomised trials and 11 observational comparisons. Remote follow-up reduced patient travel in every study that measured it, and unplanned attendances were similar where reported. Safety outcomes such as infection were rarely defined in advance. Two studies reported costs to the health service, neither with an analysis of uncertainty. No study included an economic evaluation from the patient perspective. Most studies were at serious risk of bias from historical comparison groups.

records.title: Unit costs of outpatient pain clinic activity: a micro-costing study
records.abstract: We observed 312 outpatient pain clinic contacts with time-and-motion methods and combined staff time with salary, overhead and room costs to estimate a cost per contact. A nurse-led telephone review cost 21 per contact, a nurse clinic appointment 64 and a consultant appointment 148 at 2021 prices. Overheads made up 38 percent of the cost of a clinic appointment. A telephone contact that led to a same-day clinic review cost the sum of both contacts. The estimates came from one hospital and exclude patient and companion costs.

records.title: Aftercare during spinal cord stimulation trials: a consensus statement from a national neuromodulation nursing forum
records.abstract: A panel of 14 neuromodulation nurses and physicians reached consensus on aftercare during the trial of spinal cord stimulation using two rounds of structured voting. The panel recommends that every patient has a named contact for the trial week, a wound check by day 3 either in person or by a structured remote review, and an in-person review before lead removal. The panel found no comparative evidence on the timing of wound checks and did not consider costs. Recommendations on remote review assume that the patient can use a telephone and describe the wound.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Replacing a mid-trial clinic visit with a structured nurse telephone review was not followed by more unplanned attendances in one before-after evaluation (11 of 102 against 12 of 97), and a randomised trial after interventional procedures found telephone follow-up non-inferior for satisfaction with half the clinician time. Trial infections are usually noticed after day 5 and reported by the patient, so the day 3 visit is not where they are found. A micro-costing study prices a telephone review at about a third of a nurse clinic appointment, and patient travel and companion costs are substantial. No study has combined health service and patient costs with an honest account of uncertainty.
response.gradeRationale: One uncontrolled before-after evaluation, one randomised trial in a related but different follow-up setting, a review of mostly historical comparisons and single-site costing; consistent in direction but indirect and at risk of bias.
response.summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; five source-derived claims with passages; overall certainty low.

response.reading: The day 3 visit sits between two costs that matter: clinic and nurse time on the service side and travel and lost work on the patient side. The retrieved evidence suggests that the visit rarely finds problems, because infections appear later and are reported by patients, so the risk of the change is shifted consequences (same-day reviews, emergency attendances) rather than missed infections. The evaluation has to count both sides and keep the consequences visible next to the costs.

response.rationale: The pathway change is already approved for every patient, so the useful question is what it costs and what follows from it, not whether it works in a controlled sense. A cost-consequence analysis compares the 2026 and 2027 trial episodes from the health service and patient perspectives, lists unplanned attendances, infections and on-time implant decisions beside the costs (claims c1 and c2), prices contacts with local unit costs (claim c3 gives the planning values), and counts travel and companion time, which the retrieved evidence suggests is the larger share (claim c4). response.overview: Cost-consequence analysis of a pathway change in a regional pain service, comparing all percutaneous spinal cord stimulator trial episodes started in 2026 (in-person day 3 visit) with those started in 2027 (structured nurse telephone review on day 3), from the health service and patient perspectives.
response.population: All adults starting a percutaneous spinal cord stimulator trial between 1 January 2026 and 31 December 2027; about 88 episodes a year. Episodes are analysed in the pathway of their start date whatever the patient chose on day 3.
response.exposure: 2027 pathway: a nurse telephone review on day 3 with a wound and symptom checklist and a same-day clinic slot when anything is flagged; in-person day 3 remains available on request. 2026 pathway: an in-person day 3 clinic visit. Both keep the in-person day 8 review and lead removal.
response.procedures: Resource use per episode is taken from the pain service records (contacts, same-day reviews, extra visits), the hospital emergency department system (attendances within the trial week and 30 days after lead removal) and theatre records (re-siting or early removal). Unit costs come from finance memo FIN-PM-2026-14. Patient and companion costs are estimated for both years from postcode distance, a per-kilometre rate and the proportion of companions losing a working day; in 2027 a short optional questionnaire at day 8 checks the estimate.

response.theoreticalFramework: No behavioural framework; the analysis follows the cost-consequence format with CHEERS 2022 reporting.

response.designSummary: Comparison of two consecutive annual groups of trial episodes; costs per episode summarised by mean with bootstrap intervals; consequences as proportions with exact intervals.
response.sampleSize: The sample is fixed by activity: about 88 episodes a year gives about 176. With a standard deviation of episode cost of about 110 (a planning value from the spread of contact costs; the observed value replaces it), the 95 percent confidence interval for the difference in mean cost has a half-width of about 33 (110 times the square root of 2/88, times 1.96). The expected saving of about 43 per episode (one nurse clinic slot at 64 less one call at 21, claim c3) would therefore be distinguishable from zero if it holds. Unplanned attendances near 11 percent give a half-width of about 9 percentage points for the difference, so consequences are described, not tested.
response.primaryAnalysis: Difference in mean health service cost per episode (2027 minus 2026) with a 95 percent bias-corrected bootstrap interval from 2,000 resamples. Costs in 2026 prices; no discounting within a trial week.
response.secondaryAnalysis: The same analysis for patient and companion costs and for the two perspectives combined; proportions with exact intervals for on-time implant decisions, unplanned attendances and infections; deterministic sensitivity analyses varying nurse time per call by half and double, the same-day review rate, the per-kilometre rate and the proportion of companions losing a working day; restriction to single-lead trials.
response.missingData: Missing resource items are counted as missing, never as zero; episodes with missing emergency department linkage are reported and analysed in a sensitivity analysis that assumes the 2026 attendance rate.
response.multiplicity: One primary comparison; everything else is presented as a cost-consequence table with intervals and no significance claims.
response.software: R with the boot package; costing spreadsheet and analysis script archived before the 2027 data are opened.
overfittingGuards: Resource list and unit costs fixed before analysis
No adjustment model beyond the pre-specified single-lead restriction
response.summary: About 176 episodes give a half-width of about 33 for the cost difference; consequences are reported descriptively with intervals.

response.risks: Minimal for the evaluation itself, which uses routine records. The pathway change carries the clinical risk of a missed problem, which the balancing measures watch; the evaluation must not delay reporting such problems to the clinical team.
response.consent: No individual consent is sought for routine records under the service evaluation determination; the optional day 8 questionnaire in 2027 is anonymous and says so, and returning it is voluntary.
response.data: Extraction by the nurse consultant into a password-protected spreadsheet with a study number instead of name or hospital number; postcodes are converted to distances and then deleted; the file is kept on the service's restricted drive and destroyed two years after the report.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: rural patients bear the largest travel costs and gain most from the change, while people with hearing impairment, limited English or no reliable phone signal may be poorly served by a telephone review. In-person day 3 remains available on request, interpreter telephone lines are used for calls, and costs and consequences are reported separately for patients who kept an in-person visit.
response.effectiveness: The evaluation shows whether the change lowers costs without raising unplanned attendances or infections; it does not claim effects on pain outcomes.
response.efficiency: Four hours a week of existing staff time and existing records; no new data systems.
response.costs: Staff time only; the questionnaire is printed in the clinic.
response.grants: None needed; a positive result could support a regional proposal to extend telephone follow-up after implantation.
response.partnerships: Pain service manager, finance department, two patient partners from the neuromodulation support group and the emergency department audit lead.
response.rebPath: Classified by the hospital research office as a service evaluation of routinely collected data (SE-2026-077); no REB submission is required. Any later publication follows CHEERS 2022 and the journal's policy on service evaluations.
response.limitations: Historical comparison; patient costs estimated rather than measured in 2026; rare consequences are imprecise.
response.summary: Minimal-risk service evaluation with an in-person option kept for patients poorly served by telephone and equity reporting by that group.

response.partnershipPlan: Two patient partners from the neuromodulation support group review the telephone checklist wording and the questionnaire; the emergency department audit lead checks how trial-related attendances are identified.
response.socialListening: No social media listening; the support group's newsletter comments from the past year are read for mentions of trial-week travel.

response.title: Replacing the day 3 clinic visit with a nurse telephone review during spinal cord stimulator trials: a cost-consequence analysis
response.abstract: Objective: to compare health service and patient costs and the consequences of replacing the in-person day 3 visit during percutaneous spinal cord stimulator trials with a structured nurse telephone review. Design: cost-consequence analysis comparing all trial episodes in 2026 and 2027 in one regional pain service. Outcomes: health service cost per episode (primary), patient and companion costs, on-time implant decisions, unplanned attendances and infections. Results and conclusions will follow the 2027 data.
response.introduction: Trial-week visits cost patients long journeys and companions' working days, and retrieved studies suggest that a mid-trial visit rarely finds problems that patients do not report themselves. No published evaluation has costed the change from the patient perspective.
response.methods: All trial episodes started in 2026 and 2027 are included. Resource use comes from service, emergency department and theatre records, priced with local unit costs; patient costs are estimated from postcode distance in both years. The primary analysis is the difference in mean health service cost with a bootstrap interval; consequences are tabulated beside costs. The evaluation was classified as a service evaluation.
response.results: No data have been analysed yet. The report will present case mix by year, the cost-consequence table for both perspectives, bootstrap intervals and the sensitivity analyses named in the protocol.
response.discussion: The discussion will weigh any saving against the consequences, compare the result with the retrieved before-after and randomised evidence, and state whether the pathway should extend to implant follow-up.
response.limitations: Historical comparison; patient costs estimated rather than measured before the change; one service; rare consequences imprecise.
response.conclusion: To be written after analysis; it will not claim effects on pain outcomes or on the permanent implant rate.
response.summary: CHEERS-structured draft with results left empty until the 2027 data are analysed.

path.problem.rawNeed:
I am the nurse consultant for neuromodulation in a regional pain management service. We run about 90 spinal cord stimulator trials a year. After the temporary leads are placed, patients go home for seven days and come back twice: a clinic visit on day 3 for a wound check and programming questions, and a visit on day 8 to review their pain diary, decide about a permanent implant and remove the leads. Many of our patients travel more than an hour each way, often with a relative who takes a day off work, and the day 3 visit rarely changes anything: last year it led to a change in management for 9 of 88 patients, mostly reprogramming that could have been done by phone.

From January 2027 we are replacing the day 3 visit with a structured telephone call from a neuromodulation nurse, using a wound and symptom checklist and a same-day review slot if anything is flagged. The day 8 visit stays in person. The service manager has asked whether this saves money once nurse time, missed problems and extra visits are counted, and whether it simply moves costs onto patients, families or other services such as the emergency department.

We would like to do an economic evaluation of the change, comparing patients treated in the year before with patients treated in the year after, from both the health service and the patient perspective. I need help choosing which costs and consequences to measure, how to handle infections and unplanned visits, what sample we will realistically have, and how to present the uncertainty honestly to a manager who wants one number.
